report.answer_text:
TikTok briefly went dark in the U.S. in January 2025, then stayed online while the Trump administration repeatedly delayed enforcement of a federal divest-or-ban law. ByteDance signed a deal in December, but the ownership change didn’t close until January 22, 2026. (apnews.com)
January–February: The Supreme Court upheld the law on January 17. TikTok went offline late January 18 and restored service on January 19 after Trump promised to delay enforcement. He signed the order on January 20, but TikTok didn’t return to Apple’s and Google’s U.S. app stores until February 13. (supremecourt.gov)
April–September: Trump extended the enforcement pause several times. On September 25, he signed an executive order approving a framework for a majority American-owned U.S. joint venture and giving the parties more time to close the deal. (govinfo.gov)
December and the closing: On December 18, TikTok told employees it had signed binding agreements with Oracle, Silver Lake, and MGX. When the deal closed in January 2026, those three investors each held 15% of TikTok USDS Joint Venture LLC, and ByteDance retained 19.9%. (fidelity.com)
It wasn’t a sale of TikTok worldwide. The joint venture took responsibility for U.S. user data, recommendation-algorithm security, and content moderation, while U.S. users remained connected to the global platform. TikTok’s global business also kept certain commercial functions, including advertising and e-commerce. (newsroom.tiktok.com)

It will be majority-owned and controlled by United States persons and will no longer be controlled by any foreign adversary, since ByteDance Ltd. and its affiliates will own less than 20 percent of the entity
